1) Pick a profitable STEM major. Computer Science, MIS, Accounting, Chemistry, you get the idea.

2) Go to community college for your gen eds, then an in-state state school to finish your degree. Keep your costs as low as possible. College is an investment, NOT a party or experience or whatever baloney college recruiters try to tell you.

3) Live substantially within your means. Don't take on debt for anything besides a house (after all other debt paid off), or college (and keep that spending as low as possible). No, you dont need to take a trip overseas. No, you dont need a new car.

4) Save an emergency fund. This needs to be able to cover your health insurance max OoP initially, and after you graduate you should save 3-6 months of living expenses as an emergency fund.

5) Do not major in liberal arts. Incase STEM major wasnt a clear enough hint, you want a /NERD/ career. Not majoring undergrad business. Not Transgender-Asian-American Studies. Not freakin English.

6) Learn to differentiate between needs and wants. You need clothes you can wear to work. You need food. You need bare bones housing. Needs will involve death or starving on the street if you do not meet them. You do NOT need a brand new car, spending $100/mo on your cell phone plan, cable tv, a fancy house to impress your friends, etc. Buying wants isn't wrong, but you have to prioritize: Needs > savings > wants.

What works for me is having data in useful ways to be reviewed about your spending habits, and cash flows. Find a budgeting tool that can categorize all your transactions for you, and tally your spending in different areas. This will allow you to see where all your money goes on a monthly basis, and if you have any problem areas that need to be addressed. I personally use Mint to do this, since they link with many online banking/credit/loan/etc. services to automatically grab your transaction data, categorize it, and provide sometimes useful graphs of different things.

But that's all just looking at how you spend your money. The real solution to not being in debt for your whole life, like @A6-EGO said, is to not spend more than you have (or make). I like to think about my finances in terms of rates of flow. You earn income at a certain rate, and your lifestyle burns money at a certain rate. Keep your monthly burn below your monthly income and you'll be fine.
